body:
## Question

Which hosting and ownership architecture can fulfill the agreed single-window navigation contract while preserving independent project workspaces and the existing Agents experience?

Use the chat-ownership and tab-lifecycle decisions and the Electron research. Trace the candidate through the existing code's native-window identity, workspace configuration/storage/trust, profiles/extensions, terminals/tasks/debuggers, remote authority, chat providers, layout/focus, menus, and application shutdown.

Decide where the shared shell lives, how workbenches are hosted, how a selected project/chat is targeted, and which state has one owner versus a project-local owner. Respect the current layer direction (`vs/sessions` may import `vs/workbench`, not the reverse) or explicitly justify changing it. Avoid parallel transcript/state stores for the same conversation.

Resolve with a proposed architecture and a bounded, disposable runtime experiment capable of accepting or falsifying it on macOS, with the limits of cross-platform and remote evidence stated. Create the now-specifiable feasibility ticket(s) before declaring the architecture validated. The destination requires an evidence-backed feasibility decision, not only plausible API documentation.

Inputs: [Define project ownership and navigation for chats](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/17); [Define project tab lifecycle and background activity](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/18); [Assess Electron support for live workbenches in one window](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/19).

comments.body:
## Resolution

The creator selected BrowserWindow with retained views, then explicitly accepted the proposed hosting ownership, conversation ownership, and staged experiment ("Yes to all"). This resolves the architecture candidate to test. It does not establish runtime feasibility or authorize production implementation.

### Selected hosting and ownership

Use one native BrowserWindow whose primary renderer presents the shared shell. Retain the real Agents workbench and each independent project workbench in separate WebContentsViews. Switching selects, sizes, shows, and focuses the appropriate view without rebuilding its workspace or stopping background work.

| Owner | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Shared shell | Permanent Agents navigation, project tabs and order, selected view, stable shell profile/theme, and presentation of aggregate attention. It does not own project service containers or conversation transcripts. |
| Main-process hosting support | Native window, view attachment/bounds, authenticated renderer-to-workbench-to-host mapping, native focus/menu routing, and coordination of workbench close/reload versus host shutdown. |
| Each project workbench | Its workspace configuration, workspace storage and trust context, workspace-associated profile, extensions, editors/layout, Git, terminals, tasks, debugging, and remote connection/authority. Existing application-wide and shared-profile scopes remain shared rather than being copied per tab. |
| Persistent Agents environment | Existing Sessions model/provider orchestration and Agents presentation, with its own stable profile/theme. It remains available while project views are active and after project closure. |
| Each conversation's existing provider | Authoritative conversation identity, transcript, execution and recovery. Agents and project chat editors access that authority; they do not create competing persistent conversation stores. |

The renderer bootstrap must distinguish a hosted workbench identity from the native host-window identity. Preserve durable workspace identity separately, using the exact workspace and environment agreed in [Define project ownership and navigation for chats](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/17#issuecomment-6456724688). Do not give every renderer the shell's window ID or invent IDs without updating native lookup and message destinations. Bind privileged operations to the authenticated sender and its registered workbench; an arbitrary caller-supplied ID is not authority.

Shared native hosting belongs at the existing platform/native-window boundary. Provider-neutral chat view/command contracts belong in shared Workbench or lower layers, with Sessions-owned implementations/adapters. Compose the shell and concrete workbench entry points above those shared contracts. Preserve `vs/sessions` → `vs/workbench`; no reverse imports or provider implementations imported by shared consumers. Retain sandbox/preload and IPC validation boundaries. An Electron session partition is not workspace, trust, or profile isolation.

### Navigation and commands

- Project selection routes project commands, status, extension-host connections and native menu actions to that workbench. Focusing the native host must restore the selected view rather than always focusing the shell's primary web contents. In Agents, project-specific actions need an explicit project target as already agreed.
- Chat navigation carries the owning provider, session resource and exact chat resource together with the recorded home workspace. Consumers do not parse provider URI formats or substitute the session's main chat. Resolve/open the exact home tab, then reveal the exact chat editor; apply the existing unavailable-home recovery rules.
- Each project retains its own layout and focus history. The shell coordinates view bounds and transitions without mixing project DOM/service containers. Keyboard-only navigation, dialogs, IME and hidden-view accessibility are runtime acceptance checks.

### Same conversation, two presentations

The persistent Agents environment coordinates each conversation's existing provider through a provider-neutral interface that project chat editors can consume. Renderer-local chat models may project that authority for rendering; they must not become a second transcript persistence or request-execution owner. Navigation attaches to the existing conversation and does not implicitly claim its tool execution, resend a request, or answer an approval.

Preserve unsent input, attachments, model choices, reading position, streaming state and pending approvals across navigation. Reuse provider-owned synchronization where it exists. Presentation state needs an explicit cross-renderer handoff, including rapid switches before a debounced draft write completes; a second conversation store is not that handoff. Send, cancel and approval mutations route to the owning provider with the exact chat identity.

Required tool/client resources must outlive a project tab when its agent is running. The persistent owner must retain or acquire the necessary execution resources before project teardown; the experiment must demonstrate how this works with the selected provider. Keeping the entire supposedly closed project workbench alive does not count as satisfying project closure. A live backend that has lost its tool executor or approval observer also fails. Project close must not silently cancel the agent or broaden its existing workspace/trust permissions.

This contract is provider-neutral, but current evidence is not provider-wide: Agent Host has attach-versus-claim and synchronized draft machinery; Copilot Cloud also depends on backing chat/extension infrastructure. Unsupported or untested provider continuity must be reported explicitly, not inferred from an Agent Host success.

### Lifecycle

Switching retains the workbench. Project close/reload runs that project's existing save, backup/Hot Exit, terminal/task/debug and cancellation safeguards, leaving other projects and Agents usable. Failed save/backup or a veto prevents destructive teardown. Ordinary project processes stop only through the agreed confirmation flow; agent resources follow their independent lifetime. Reopening restores recoverable state without replaying commands or requests.

Host close and app quit coordinate all hosted workbenches and the persistent agent owner. A veto prevents completing the host shutdown; do not destroy child web contents before their safeguards have completed. Explicitly dispose owned views/resources after approved teardown. App quit does not promise that local agent execution survives. Keep restoration and unavailable-workspace behavior from [Define project tab lifecycle and background activity](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/18#issuecomment-6464014913).

### Evidence and limits

Code was inspected at checkout `ffd7973948bdb469993485c2662483205d983223`. These are integration constraints, not a working implementation:

- `src/vs/platform/windows/electron-main/windowImpl.ts` derives CodeWindow identity from BrowserWindow; `src/vs/platform/ipc/electron-browser/mainProcessService.ts` uses that identity for renderer IPC. `src/vs/platform/utilityProcess/electron-main/utilityProcess.ts` resolves extension-host response destinations through a native window and transfers its port to that window's primary web contents. The hosted-view route must replace this assumption.
- `src/vs/workbench/electron-browser/desktop.main.ts` builds the per-workbench workspace, storage, trust, profile and remote services. This supports retaining independent workbenches rather than replacing one workbench's workspace on every switch.
- `src/vs/platform/menubar/electron-main/menubar.ts` and `src/vs/platform/lifecycle/electron-main/lifecycleMainService.ts` route through native windows. They need distinct selected-workbench command routing and per-workbench shutdown coordination.
- `src/vs/sessions/SESSIONS.md` defines provider/model orchestration separately from presentation. `src/vs/workbench/contrib/chat/browser/agentSessions/agentHost/agentHostSessionHandler.ts` distinguishes attaching from claiming, synchronizes drafts, and exposes the danger of tools waiting for an approval observer. `src/vs/sessions/contrib/chat/browser/chatViewStateService.ts` currently caches view state within one renderer.
- [Assess Electron support for live workbenches in one window](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/19#issuecomment-6456243516) supplies version-pinned documentary evidence for view composition. Separate web contents do not guarantee separate renderer processes or crash isolation.

### Feasibility gate and handoff

Use the already-created [Validate the selected hosting architecture with live workbenches](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/23), refined with the staged acceptance checks. First prove real hosting, isolation, command routing and lifecycle with Agents and two local projects; then exact-chat/tool continuity and the agreed workload measurements. Stop and return the candidate for revision when a required invariant fails rather than concealing it behind mocked services or a simulated workbench.

The macOS experiment must record the actual build/runtime, evidence, failure modes, measurements, provider coverage and creator review. Warm switching targets roughly 200 ms; measure memory and CPU at 3–5 and ten projects without automatically closing or suspending them. Untested providers, Windows/Linux, SSH and Dev Containers remain explicitly unvalidated. Remote authority isolation remains an architecture constraint even in a local-only experiment.

The existing migration decision owns old-window restoration and compatibility. The existing interaction prototype owns the clickable product review. Neither those decisions nor the runtime experiment are resolved here. Final specification approval remains blocked by their native dependencies. No new ticket is needed: the existing children cover all now-specifiable follow-up work, and no new domain term or production specification is introduced by this resolution.

## Returned for refinement after creator review

The creator agreed with the [first runtime experiment’s assessment](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/23#issuecomment-6464741371): retain BrowserWindow plus retained WebContentsViews as the candidate, but refine IPC ownership before rerunning. Initial rendering succeeded; the sender-binding gate failed in the incomplete adapter. This is not a rejection of the hosting primitive or the agreed product contract.

Reopen this decision to specify the native-service boundary concretely: how authenticated WebContents map to logical workbench identity, where that identity is enforced across IPC/service proxies, which explicit cross-workbench operations are permitted and by whom, and how stale/disposed targets are rejected. Caller-supplied IDs must not themselves grant authority. Preserve the previously accepted ownership/layering/lifecycle requirements; the original resolution remains historical context.

[Revalidate live workbench hosting after IPC refinement](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/25) is a child of the map and is natively blocked by this decision. It carries the full original staged acceptance contract. Final specification approval is natively blocked by both this reopened decision and that follow-up experiment.

This comment scopes the next decision; it does not resolve the IPC design on the creator’s behalf.

## Resolution — authenticated native-service boundary

The creator explicitly accepted the coordinator permissions and stale-target behavior, then accepted the caller-identity recommendation after a plain-language explanation: “Yes go with your recommendation.” This resolves the reopened design decision, not runtime feasibility.

Retain the BrowserWindow with retained WebContentsViews candidate and all ownership, conversation, layering, and lifecycle requirements in the [original architecture resolution](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/20#issuecomment-6464249932). This refinement specifies the missing IPC boundary.

### Identity and enforcement

The main process owns a registry binding each actual Electron WebContents and its current renderer/document connection lifetime to its logical workbench, native host window, role, and lifecycle state. Native host identity, logical workbench identity, and durable workspace identity remain distinct. The main process establishes the binding when creating/registering the renderer; neither a caller-supplied method argument nor the generic IPC handshake context establishes authority.

Enforce that binding at the main-process service-channel boundary, before dispatching native service calls or registering event subscriptions. Own-workbench operations derive their destination from the authenticated binding. An ID purporting to identify another caller must reject rather than impersonate it. Explicit target selectors are checked against the permissions of that operation; possessing an ID grants no permission. Event subscriptions must likewise expose only the caller's permitted scope.

Keep the enforcement at the shared platform/native hosting boundary, preserving `vs/sessions` → `vs/workbench`. Classify native-service methods and subscriptions by scope before exposing them through the hosted adapter; fixing only the PID method or trusting the generic proxy context is insufficient. Preserve existing application-wide capabilities under explicit scope rather than treating all services as project-local. Internal/shared-process connections have their own main-established role; they must not acquire authority by claiming a renderer identity. Auxiliary-window targets require a registered ownership relationship.

Extension-host ports, replies and renderer-targeted IPC use the same registered destination and lifetime. Authorization must precede port transfer or side effects; correctly routing to a supplied ID alone is not sufficient.

### Permitted coordination

- The shell may request project selection, opening, closing and reloading through named coordinator operations. Close/reload still run the agreed save, backup, running-work and veto safeguards.
- Agents may request exact-chat navigation to the recorded home workspace. Project workbenches may request the agreed navigation actions through the coordinator. These are explicit operations, not unrestricted access to another project's native services.
- Conversation mutations continue through the owning provider with the exact conversation identity; navigation grants no transcript, execution or approval ownership.
- Main-process native-menu handling targets the selected workbench through the coordinator. Selection is routing information for those actions, never authentication for background requests.

### Stale and disposed targets

Close, crash, reload or document replacement invalidates the old lifetime's connections, subscriptions and pending deliveries. Reload registers a fresh binding. Reject foreign, unknown or stale targets explicitly before effects or port transfer; never fall back to the active project or silently deliver a stale response into a new renderer. An already-started operation is not promised to roll back: retain its existing cancellation/error semantics, but do not redirect its result. Disposal remains subject to the previously agreed lifecycle safeguards.

### Evidence and next gate

Read-only inspection confirms that Electron receives the actual WebContents in `src/vs/base/parts/ipc/electron-main/ipc.electron.ts`, while generic IPC deserializes client-provided context in `src/vs/base/parts/ipc/common/ipc.ts`. The native-host client prepends its window ID in `src/vs/platform/native/common/nativeHostService.ts`; the generic service proxy dispatches supplied arguments. These are integration facts, not new runtime results. The [first experiment](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/23#issuecomment-6464741371) demonstrated the missing binding with a cross-workbench PID query.

[Revalidate live workbench hosting after IPC refinement](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/25) owns implementation and validation of the disposable adapter. Its first gate must test spoofed argument IDs and handshake context, explicit/nested targets, event visibility, extension-host port and reply destinations, legitimate coordinator operations, and reload/disposal races. Then run the remaining original staged contract without waiving any check, including investigation of the prior Agents extension-host restart.

No production implementation or specification change is made here. This boundary is not a complete project security sandbox. Provider continuity, performance, lifecycle, remote runtime and cross-platform feasibility remain unvalidated. The existing follow-up experiment covers all newly specified work; no duplicate ticket or product glossary term is needed. Final specification approval remains blocked by runtime validation.

## Returned for document-generation and revocation refinement

The [second runtime experiment](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/25#issuecomment-6465346507) implemented main-authenticated caller binding and passed the sampled caller/handshake spoofing checks, but failed the required renderer-lifetime gate. After reload, a new renderer connection could dispatch an operation on an extension-host handle issued before reload. Captured Electron main-frame identity did not provide a sufficient generation boundary.

Retain the previously accepted hosting candidate and product contract as the starting point. Refine the concrete main-owned document/connection generation and resource revocation contract: when generations are created/invalidated, how handles and subscriptions are bound to them, and how asynchronous service effects and deliveries reject stale generations. This is a refinement prompted by an incomplete adapter, not a finding that Electron composition is impossible.

Reopening follows the experiment's instruction to return a failed required invariant for revision. The creator has not yet reviewed or accepted this experiment's verdict; [Revalidate live workbench hosting after IPC refinement](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/25) remains open for that review and still carries the complete staged acceptance obligation. No new architecture decision is resolved here.

## Resolution — main-owned generations and resource revocation

The creator explicitly accepted both parts of this refinement: renderer cleanup preserves provider-owned agents with fresh authorized access and generation checks, and the main process issues a fresh generation for each replacement renderer, revoking old access before approved replacement and immediately on crash or destruction. A vetoed reload leaves current access intact.

Retain the hosting candidate and all ownership, layering, authorization and lifecycle requirements in the [original architecture resolution](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/20#issuecomment-6464249932) and [authenticated native-service boundary](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/20#issuecomment-6465039246). This resolves the design refinement, not runtime feasibility.

### Generation and connection contract

The main process owns the current document generation for each registered logical workbench. Allocate a fresh, non-reused generation for initial creation and each replacement document; do not infer continuity from WebContents or WebFrameMain identity. Bind authenticated connections to their document generation when registering them. Connections have their own lifetime within that generation: closing one invalidates its access and pending deliveries, and reconnecting does not revive it. Client-supplied generation or connection identifiers grant no authority.

For an approved reload or close, first complete existing save/backup/running-work safeguards and veto handling, then invalidate the outgoing generation before replacement or teardown begins. A veto leaves the current generation usable. Crash, destruction, or actual document replacement invalidates old access immediately; an unexpected replacement must not inherit it. Same-document activity and project-tab switching do not themselves replace the document generation.

The adapter must establish the replacement document's binding through a main-controlled bootstrap, rejecting old or ambiguous connections during transition. The exact Electron hooks/bootstrap wiring must be demonstrated by the experiment; a new counter attached to an unauthenticated handshake is not sufficient.

### Resources, subscriptions and asynchronous work

Bind renderer-owned handles and subscriptions to the authenticated workbench, document generation and relevant connection lifetime. Revoke old handles, detach subscriptions, cancel pending work where supported, and dispose renderer-owned resources. A fresh connection cannot use a handle from before reload even if its logical workbench is unchanged. Preserve existing operation scopes and reject foreign, unknown and stale authority before dispatch.

Pending operations retain their originating binding. Recheck that binding before further asynchronous service effects, resource publication, event delivery, replies or port transfers. A late-created renderer-owned resource must be cleaned up if its originating lifetime has expired. Never deliver a stale result or port to the replacement renderer or fall back to the selected project. Effects already completed are not promised to roll back; preserve existing cancellation/error semantics.

### Independent agent lifetime

Revoking renderer access is separate from terminating provider-owned agents. Renderer-owned resources are cleaned up; provider-owned agents continue under their existing permissions and authoritative conversation owner. Replacement renderers obtain fresh authorized access rather than inheriting old handles. Navigation or reattachment does not resend requests or transfer execution/approval ownership implicitly.

Preserve the prior requirement that necessary agent tools and approval observation survive project closure through an independent owner. Keeping the closed project renderer alive is not a substitute. This contract does not broaden provider permissions or establish provider-wide continuity.

### Validation and handoff

[Revalidate live workbench hosting after lifetime revocation refinement](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/26) owns the disposable implementation and complete staged validation. Start with the stale extension-host handle reproduction, then cover generation transitions, vetoes, connection replacement, pending effects/deliveries and resource cleanup alongside legitimate fresh access. Preserve all earlier native-service, coordinator, isolation, lifecycle, provider, usability and capacity checks.

No new runtime evidence is claimed. The existing experiment covers the now-specified work, so no duplicate ticket is needed. No production code, authoritative specification or product glossary is changed: document generations and connection lifetimes are implementation concepts. Final specification approval remains blocked by runtime validation.

## Reopened — authenticate direct lifecycle replies

[Revalidate live workbench hosting after lifetime revocation refinement](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/26) found a required isolation failure. [Report and reproduction](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/blob/1c66e15dd5364d4aefc0e7f011c513567f9817d9/prototypes/live-hosting/lifetime-revocation/README.md).

The sampled stale-handle reproduction now rejects, but another project renderer could cancel the target project's real pending reload through its separate lifecycle callback. These listeners validate origin but ignore workbench/document ownership.

Refine `onBeforeUnload`/`onWillUnload` response ownership and inventory direct Electron IPC paths outside generic service authentication. Bind replies to the authorized workbench, document generation and pending operation. Reject foreign, stale, duplicate and transition-time replies without consuming another workbench's listener; define cleanup on lifetime expiry. Preserve actual save/backup/veto semantics and prove legitimate replies alongside rejections.

This stays within the accepted product and provider-permission contracts. The experiment awaits creator verdict review; reopening does not record a new accepted decision or establish feasibility.

## Resolution — direct lifecycle reply ownership and shutdown ordering

The creator explicitly accepted both proposed refinements (“Yes to both”): authenticate lifecycle replies before consuming their listener, and preserve outgoing-document access through veto and shutdown cleanup before revocation. This resolves the reopened architecture decision, not runtime feasibility or the preceding experiment's pending verdict review.

Retain the hosting, ownership, layering and provider contracts in the [original architecture resolution](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/20#issuecomment-6464249932), [authenticated native-service boundary](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/20#issuecomment-6465039246), and [main-owned generations and resource revocation](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/20#issuecomment-6465585830). The ordering below makes the last contract precise.

### Reply ownership

Main owns each pending close/reload operation and its expected lifecycle phase. Accept before-unload OK/cancel and will-unload completion only from the authenticated logical workbench and exact document generation that received that operation, for the currently expected phase. Caller-supplied window IDs, generation claims and knowledge of a callback channel are not authority.

Validate ownership and operation/phase before consuming the listener or settling the operation. Reject foreign, stale, guessed, duplicate and invalid transition-time replies without removing or settling the legitimate pending wait. A valid phase response is consumed once; subsequent replies cannot affect another phase or operation. Preserve existing origin, frame and payload validation as well as this ownership check.

Apply the same scope and ownership review to direct Electron IPC outside generic service authentication. Classify legitimate project, shell, auxiliary and internal roles explicitly rather than granting every renderer shared authority or denying every application-wide operation. The follow-up must inventory and test these paths, including requests, delayed replies, ports and callbacks.

### Shutdown ordering and interruption

Keep the outgoing document's existing authorized access valid through both before-unload veto handling and will-unload cleanup. Shutdown joiners must be able to complete actual save, backup/storage and resource cleanup. After the authorized final cleanup acknowledgement, revoke the outgoing generation before replacement or native teardown begins. A veto preserves current access. This does not extend a connection that independently closes or broaden any existing permissions.

If the renderer crashes, is destroyed or is unexpectedly replaced during either phase, invalidate its lifetime immediately and retire its pending callbacks as an interrupted operation. Never synthesize approval/completion from silence or let a replacement document finish the old operation. Preserve the existing crash/unresponsive recovery and user safeguards; a pending wait must not silently hang after its owning lifetime has ended. Already completed effects are not promised to roll back.

Renderer cleanup remains separate from independently provider-owned agent lifetime. Preserve the previous agent, tool and approval continuity contract without duplicating execution or conversation ownership.

### Evidence and follow-up

Read-only source inspection found that lifecycle reply handlers ignore sender ownership, and that the validated IPC wrapper's one-shot listener is consumed before its validation callback runs. Main waits for before-unload then will-unload; the renderer waits for shutdown joiners before replying. These are source findings, not new runtime results. The observed cross-project cancellation remains evidence from the [preceding experiment report](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/26#issuecomment-6466421164).

[Revalidate live workbench hosting after lifecycle reply authorization](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/27) owns the disposable implementation and complete staged rerun. Demonstrate authorized veto and successful cleanup alongside foreign/stale/duplicate/transition rejection, listener preservation, unexpected lifetime expiry and fresh replacement isolation. Inventory other direct IPC paths and preserve every inherited gate. No duplicate ticket is needed.

No production code, authoritative specification or glossary is changed. Runtime feasibility, provider continuity, cross-platform and remote acceptance remain unvalidated. The preceding experiment remains open for its separate creator verdict review; acceptance of this architecture refinement does not close it.

## Runtime evidence requires recovery-ownership revision

[Revalidate live workbench hosting after lifecycle reply authorization](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/27) now has [disposable runtime evidence](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/blob/e227996f44b/prototypes/live-hosting/lifecycle-replies/README.md): sampled reply authorization and legitimate save/cancel/reload work, but a project crash followed by native Reopen destroys the shared BrowserWindow and exits Agents' and the neighbouring project's extension hosts. Stage 1 stopped; feasibility remains unvalidated and creator experiment review is pending.

Reopened this decision to specify the boundary between logical project recovery/teardown and native host close/quit. The current inherited `CodeWindow.destroyWindow()` opens a replacement then destroys its `_win` (the shared host); process lifecycle listeners also observe native `closed`. Define how recovery replaces only the failed workbench/document, clears stale view/registry/resource ownership, keeps the host and neighbours usable, and preserves safeguards, provider-owned work and exact-chat ownership. No accepted interaction contract is waived, and no new design resolution is inferred from this report.

## Resolution — narrow ownership split for project recovery

The creator accepted: “Let’s go with the narrow ownership split. Keep recovery confined to the failed project, with Retry and Close if it fails, and update the decision and follow-up experiment.” This resolves the reopened architecture decision, not runtime feasibility.

Retain BrowserWindow plus retained WebContentsViews and the [original ownership and lifecycle contract](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/20#issuecomment-6464249932), [authenticated native-service boundary](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/20#issuecomment-6465039246), [main-owned generations and resource revocation](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/20#issuecomment-6465585830), and [lifecycle reply ownership and shutdown ordering](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/20#issuecomment-6467262466).

### Ownership and recovery

The main-process host coordinator alone owns intentional destruction of the shared native window. Each logical project workbench owns its hosted view and project-scoped resources. Project close, reload and crash recovery must not destroy the shared host or trigger neighbouring workbench cleanup. Native host close/quit coordinates the existing safeguards across hosted workbenches and the independent agent owner before destructive teardown.

Recovery targets the failed project's exact workspace/environment and tab identity. Retire the failed document's access, pending callbacks and renderer-owned resources under the accepted generation rules; detach/dispose its old view and retire stale registry entries and listeners exactly once. Repair view selection and routing as needed. Bootstrap only its replacement with fresh authorized access. Healthy projects, Agents and the shell remain usable, and their resources must not be stopped by that recovery. A replacement restores recoverable state and reconnects surviving work without replaying commands, agent requests or approvals or creating another conversation owner.

Apply this distinction throughout logical close/destroy notifications, window bookkeeping/restoration, extension-host and utility-process cleanup, and native close/quit coordination. Replacing one native destroy call is insufficient. Preserve project save/backup, veto and running-work safeguards for live close/reload; a crashed renderer cannot supply a fabricated successful cleanup acknowledgement. Independent provider-owned work retains its existing owner and permissions.

### Failed recovery and races

If replacement fails, keep the project tab identifiable with Retry and Close while other views remain usable. Preserve recoverable backups. Never automatically restart or destroy the shared window as a fallback. Closing the failed tab follows the existing tab-selection and surviving-resource safeguards.

Allow only one recovery operation at a time per project. Coordinate it with project Close and host shutdown; invalidate late completions so repeated Retry cannot create duplicate replacements, revive stale access, or resurrect a closed tab. Use existing services and lifecycle mechanisms for this bounded ownership split. No general recovery framework, automatic retry policy, configurable recovery modes or new recovery subsystem is required.

Distinguish project renderer failure from Agents/shell renderer failure and actual native-host loss; route prompts and actions to the affected owner. The requirement is that project recovery causes no collateral teardown. It does not guarantee process-level crash isolation or that provider execution survives loss of its own execution owner.

### Evidence and follow-up

The [creator-reviewed experiment](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/27#issuecomment-6467988931) failed after native Reopen: the shared BrowserWindow disappeared and neighbouring extension hosts exited. Read-only inspection at `e227996f44b1c0b1876278ef09249deeaa7b9629` confirms the integration surfaces: `windowImpl.ts` destroys shared `_win` during project recovery; logical window/lifecycle bookkeeping and utility processes also observe shared native `closed`; `prototypeWorkbenchHost.ts` lacks complete view disposal and routing repair. These are source findings and prior captured evidence, not a new runtime result.

[Revalidate live workbench hosting after recovery ownership refinement](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/28) owns the disposable implementation and full staged rerun. It must test the complete ownership boundary, failed recovery and races as well as reproduce the original failure, then preserve every inherited security, lifecycle, provider, usability and capacity gate. A local recovery success alone is not a Stage 1 pass.

No production implementation, authoritative specification or glossary change is made. Existing terms suffice. The existing follow-up covers the now-specified work; no duplicate ticket is needed. Runtime feasibility, full provider continuity, Windows/Linux, SSH and Dev Containers remain unvalidated. The separate pending review of the lifetime-revocation experiment is unchanged.

## Revision needed — Close during overlapping recovery and host shutdown

[Revalidate live workbench hosting after recovery ownership refinement](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/28) reports a scoped failed experiment, with evidence publication and the creator's verdict pending. Local project crash recovery now preserves the shared host in its sampled UI case, but Close returns without action while host shutdown and recovery overlap; after host shutdown cancels, the pending retry continues.

Retain the previously accepted ownership/authentication/lifecycle contracts. Resolve the remaining precedence question with the creator: **what happens to a project Close requested while the host is considering shutdown and that project is recovering, particularly when shutdown is vetoed?** The action must not be silently dropped. Decide when Close is accepted or visibly deferred/rejected, when pending recovery is invalidated, and how cancellation leaves surviving views usable. No general recovery framework is requested.

The current prototype drops the request via an early return on the host-busy flag. The existing contract already requires coordination; this is a concrete boundary to specify and validate, not evidence of fundamental Electron infeasibility. Do not treat this comment as an accepted replacement decision. Full staged validation and the separate creator verdict remain required.

## Resolution — Close precedence during recovery and host shutdown

The creator accepted both recommendations: “Yes—remember Close and cancel recovery” and “Yes—keep recovery cancelled until explicit Retry.” This resolves the reopened architecture decision, not runtime feasibility.

Retain the [narrow recovery ownership split](https://github.com/ejjsharpe/escode/issues/20#issuecomment-6468194501) and its inherited authentication, generation, lifecycle, provider and ownership contracts.

### Accept Close and retain its intent

Accept an authorized project Close even while that project is recovering and the host is considering shutdown. Main records one pending Close for that exact logical project, immediately invalidates its pending recovery, and exposes “Close pending.” Repeated Close requests coalesce; Retry is unavailable while Close is pending. The shell, native recovery dialog and service entry points must follow the same rule rather than silently returning on the host-busy flag.

Cancelling recovery invalidates its future continuations; it does not revoke a healthy outgoing document's access before its required shutdown joiners finish. Late validation, bootstrap, readiness or failure callbacks cannot attach or select an obsolete replacement, revive authority, overwrite current state or resurrect a closed tab. Clean up resources from obsolete recovery attempts. Handle replacement already underway as well as preparation not yet completed, preserving recoverable state and existing safeguards.

### Serialize teardown with the host outcome

Defer separate project teardown while host shutdown owns lifecycle coordination; do not run competing unload sequences or duplicate cleanup.

- If host shutdown succeeds, fulfil pending Close through that coordinated shutdown exactly once.
- If host shutdown is vetoed or cancelled, retain the project Close intent and complete it through normal project-close safeguards after host coordination releases ownership. Do not resume the cancelled recovery.
- If shutdown is interrupted, preserve interruption and recovery safeguards. Do not fabricate successful cleanup, lose the Close intent or blindly repeat shutdown joiners that already completed. Reconcile the actual surviving workbench/resource state before continuing the pending close; retain usable surviving views and explicit failure state where recovery is needed.

Apply this ordering both while before-unload permission is being considered and after will-unload cleanup has started. Actual native-host loss remains distinct from a cancelled shutdown; this decision does not promise execution survives loss of its owner.

### If project Close is cancelled

If the project's own safeguards veto or cancel Close, clear its pending-close state and retain the tab and recoverable data. Keep a healthy workbench usable; otherwise retain the failed tab with Retry and Close. Recovery remains cancelled until an explicit Retry. A failed close must be visible and must not silently discard the tab or restart recovery. Preserve independent provider-owned work, tool/approval continuity and exact-chat ownership under the existing contract.

## Resolution — safe project disposal and truthful Close completion

The creator accepted the recommended fix: “Ok great, lets go with that recommended fix,” after discussing the user experience and the concrete failure: cleanup reads a view that has already been destroyed and stops before bookkeeping finishes. This resolves the design refinement, not runtime feasibility.

### Bounded disposal fix

Capture the identity and ownership information needed for cleanup before destroying the hosted view. Keep logical workbench identity, hosted document lifetime and native host identity distinct after view expiry. An expired hosted project must never fall back to the shell or another project; reject stale routing and authority explicitly.

Use the existing hosting and lifecycle services to make disposal safe under repeated calls, destruction notifications and overlapping Close/recovery/host-shutdown continuations. Already-destroyed resources count as gone. Complete the remaining safe bookkeeping even if an earlier resource is unavailable; deleting one registry entry must not make a later cleanup attempt skip unfinished work. Retire owned references, subscriptions/listeners and resources, update logical registration/counts and restoration state, and repair selection/routing. Deliver logical-close notifications and completion consistently, once, without triggering shared-host or neighbouring workbench teardown. Surface real cleanup failures rather than swallowing them or claiming completion.

Preserve the accepted lifecycle ordering: a healthy outgoing document keeps its authorized access through required save/backup and shutdown joiners; revoke after acknowledged cleanup and before destructive teardown. Crash/destruction revokes access immediately and cannot fabricate acknowledgement. Preserve recoverable data, independent provider-owned agents/tools/approvals and healthy neighbouring views. Do not repeat completed unload phases, resume cancelled recovery or allow late callbacks to resurrect a tab.

### User-visible outcome

Normal Close remains unchanged. Keep Close pending until its required teardown and bookkeeping actually complete. Report success only when complete, and cancellation only for a genuine safeguard veto/cancellation. If teardown partly succeeds and then fails, preserve recoverable work, reject routing to the expired project and expose an accurate failure rather than “Close cancelled” or false success. Do not pretend a destroyed project is still usable.

No permanent cleanup-retry control, new recovery setting, automatic recovery policy or general recovery framework is accepted or required. A dedicated cleanup-retry interface may be unnecessary once the bug is fixed. Any retry of unfinished disposal must be safe and distinct from reopening/recovering the project; it must not replay completed shutdown work.

It must not alter the failed attempt's outcome, replay completed unload phases or logical-close notifications, resume cancelled recovery, or revive expired authority. Keep the attempt pending until that outcome is established, then expose it truthfully to callers and the shell. Keep healthy surviving workbenches usable; where a document has actually failed, retain its accurate recovery state and reject stale routing rather than pretending it remains usable. ## Resolution — exact-document readiness and explicit Close

The creator accepted the recommendation: “Go with your recommendation.” An explicit Close during replacement startup reports **Close interrupted** promptly while the current document's lifecycle safeguards are not ready. Merely resetting the existing ready flag is insufficient: the not-ready unload shortcut must not fabricate safeguard permission, and host coordination must not classify missing readiness as a genuine veto.
